<a id="count-by-spatial-container"></a>

### Count by spatial container

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-11-24 (Revit 2024).

**What it does:** how many of these are in each room, when the elements carry no room parameter to group by.

Counts the elements handed in, broken down by which room, MEP space or HVAC zone physically CONTAINS each one - decided by testing the element's point against the container's own boundary, not by reading a parameter. It changes nothing. **`GROUP_AND_COUNT` CANNOT DO THIS, AND THE REASON IS NOT A LIMITATION OF THAT FRAGMENT.** It groups on a parameter value, which is the right mechanism for almost everything. **Most MEP elements have no Room or Space parameter at all** - a duct, a fitting or a valve does not know which room or space it sits in, and nothing writes it there. Counting the fittings per space is this fragment's job for that reason, and not the ductwork measuring fragments'. Asking for *"how many diffusers per room"* through a parameter lookup returns one enormous group of blanks and looks like an answer. **PHASE IS NOT ONE OF THESE, AND IT IS WORTH SAYING WHY NOT.** *"Count by phase created"* looks like the same question and is not: phase IS an ordinary parameter, so `GROUP_AND_COUNT` already does it, faster and exactly. Only room, space and zone need the geometric test, and only those three are offered here. **THE ZONE IS ONE HOP FURTHER THAN THE SPACE, AND SAYS SO WHEN IT FAILS.** A zone is not tested against directly: the containing space is found first, and the zone is the one that space belongs to. So an element can miss for two distinct reasons - no space contains it, or the space that does has not been put in a zone - and those are reported as two different groups, because they are two different jobs for two different people. **Counting these by HVAC zone is a READ and it never makes a zone**: a sentence asking how many elements are in each hvac zone belongs here, not with the fragment that creates one. **THE TEST POINT IS TAKEN AT THE CONTAINER'S OWN HEIGHT, WHICH IS THE WHOLE TRICK.** A room's containment test is answered at the room's own level, and a diffuser sits at ceiling height - so testing the element's own Z reports everything as being in no room. The element's X and Y are used with the container's Z. This is the same correction the room and space filters already make, reused rather than rediscovered. **AN UNPLACED OR UNENCLOSED ROOM IS SKIPPED, NOT ASKED.** A room with no area is either not placed or not bounded; its containment test cannot mean anything, and asking it anyway is how an element gets filed under a room that does not exist on the drawing. The count of those skipped is reported, because a model full of them is the real finding. **IT IS AN ELEMENT-BY-CONTAINER SWEEP AND THAT COST IS STATED.** Every element is tested against every container to find the one that matches. On a large floor with many rooms that is real work, and it is the price of an answer no parameter carries. **LINKED MODELS ARE READ ONLY WHEN ASKED FOR (version 2, D-59).** With `includeLinks` absent this answers for this model alone, exactly as the proof measured. With it set, every loaded link is read too and `linksSearched` says how many were: set and 0 means "you asked, and none are loaded", which is a different answer from host-only. Each link's placed and enclosed rooms or spaces become containers too, asked AFTER this model's own, and a linked group is named "<link> :: <room>". The ducts are here and the rooms are in the architectural link - this is the case it exists for. **NOTHING FROM A LINK IS EVER SELECTED OR CARRIED** - the elements counted are still the ones handed in; the chain revives ids against this model, and a linked id that happens to be in use here binds an unrelated element (FRAGMENT-ISSUES row 75). Links nested inside a link are not read, and are counted in the answer. This is version 2; version 1's proof no longer describes the code, and the fragment is DRAFT until it is proved again.

### Describe elements

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-09-07 (Revit 2024).

**What it does:** what are these - the category, family name, type name and id of each element.

<a id="find-views-showing-element"></a>

### Find views showing element

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-09-07 (Revit 2024).

**What it does:** which views and sheets show this element.

Which views show a given element, and which of those views are on sheets. **This is the question to ask BEFORE changing or deleting something.** An element that appears on four issued sheets is a different decision from one that appears nowhere. Revit will not warn, and the drawings are found later by whoever is checking the set. **The sheet answer is the one that matters.** A view nobody has placed can be changed freely; a view on a sheet is a drawing somebody will receive. **It is genuinely expensive and says so.** One collector pass per view, over every view in the project. That is the honest cost of a true answer — Revit keeps no reverse index — and it is why this is a deliberate check rather than something to run in a loop.

<a id="group-and-count"></a>

### Group and count

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-11-02 (Revit 2020).

**What it does:** how many of each type, size or value there are - a set of parameter values turned into a schedule-style table.

Groups the elements given by one value - type, size, width, system, level or any parameter - and says how many are in each group, largest first: a schedule-style report without making a schedule. With a length, area or volume it totals each group too, the way a bill of quantities reads - "forty lengths of 300x150 totalling 212 metres" - and an element with no quantity is counted, never skipped and never treated as zero. Changes nothing.

<a id="measure-element-volume"></a>

### Measure element volume

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-11-02 (Revit 2020).

**What it does:** how much volume and surface area do these have.

The solid volume and surface area of each element, in cubic and square metres, plus the totals. **Surface area is the one that gets used on an MEP job.** Duct insulation, painting and lagging are all bought by the square metre, and nothing in this library could produce that number — `MEASURE_ELEMENT_LENGTHS` answers a different takeoff question and was what the search offered. **It measures the GEOMETRY, not a parameter.** Revit publishes a volume parameter on some categories and not others, and where it exists it can be stale or excluded by a setting. The solids are what the element actually is. **Version 2 lists the shape as well** - solids, faces, edges and the box in millimetres, and each edge or face when asked - all read at Fine detail. **Insulation is NOT included, and that matters for exactly the job this is for.** Insulation is a separate element wrapped around the duct, so a duct's own surface area is the bare duct. To price the lagging, measure the insulation elements — which is a different selection, not a different number.

<a id="read-element-level"></a>

### Read element level

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-10-18 (Revit 2020).

**What it does:** what level are these on, and how far above it.

Which level each element belongs to, and its offset from that level in millimetres. **The level an element is ON and the level it is NEAR are different answers, and the model only knows the first.** A duct hosted on Level 1 with a 3800 mm offset sits above Level 2's floor and still reports Level 1. That is correct and it is the answer that surprises people, so the offset is reported beside the level rather than left out - a level name on its own invites the wrong conclusion in exactly the case somebody is asking about. **Elements have more than one way of carrying a level, and they are not interchangeable.** `LevelId` is empty on plenty of MEP elements that carry their level in a parameter instead, so both are read, in a fixed order, and the answer says nothing at all rather than guessing when neither is present. **A floor, a door, a duct and a pipe each carry a level too**, and are asked which level they are on in the same words.

<a id="read-element-phase"></a>

### Read element phase

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-09-07 (Revit 2024).

**What it does:** what phase were these created in, and when are they demolished.

The phase an element was created in, and the phase it is demolished in if it is. On a refurbishment that is the difference between existing services and new ones, and it is invisible in most views. **An element has TWO phases, not one, and reading only the first is the mistake.** Created and demolished together are what say whether something is existing-to-remain, existing-to-be-demolished, or new. An element created in "Existing" reads identically to one that is also demolished in "Phase 1" until the second is read, and those are opposite instructions on site. **A view's phase filter decides what is DRAWN, not what an element IS.** Two views can show the same model completely differently, and neither changes what this reports. Somebody asking "why is this not showing" is usually asking about the view, which is a different question.

<a id="report-compound-structure"></a>

### Report compound structure

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-09-07 (Revit 2024).

**What it does:** what this wall, floor or roof is actually made of, layer by layer.

Reads the layer build-up of a wall, floor, roof or ceiling TYPE - each layer's function, material and thickness, where the core starts and stops, and the total. The *"what is this wall made of"* answer. It changes nothing. **IT EXISTS BECAUSE THE QUESTION WAS BEING ANSWERED BY `CREATE_WALL`.** Measured before this batch, *"what is the wall build up"* resolved to the fragment that BUILDS A WALL. A question about an existing type, answered by making a new element - the worst shape of mis-route in this library, and the same one `CHECK_FAMILY_STANDARDS` and `REPORT_VIEW_FILTERS` were built to close. **IT REPORTS TYPES, NOT INSTANCES, AND DEDUPES.** Nine walls of one type are one build-up, and listing it nine times buries the one thing being asked. An instance is resolved to its type; a type handed in directly is used as it is, so this works downstream of a category filter or a type filter equally. **THE CORE IS MARKED, BECAUSE IT IS WHAT DIMENSIONS AND ROOMS MEASURE TO.** Revit's core boundary decides where a wall's location line can sit, what a room boundary follows, and what a dimension to "wall face" actually hits. A layer list without the core marked reads as a plain stack and hides the one line that changes measurements. **A CURTAIN WALL AND AN IN-PLACE ELEMENT HAVE NO COMPOUND STRUCTURE, AND THAT IS AN ANSWER.** It is not an error and not an empty result. A curtain wall is made of panels and mullions instead - `REPORT_CURTAIN_ELEMENTS` is that question, and this fragment names it rather than returning nothing.

<a id="report-curtain-elements"></a>

### Report curtain elements

**DRAFT - runs in a chat, and its answer says so.** It changes nothing in the model, so it is not refused, but it has not been proved on a real model yet.

**What it does:** the panels, mullions and grid lines a curtain wall or a curtain system is actually made of.

Reads what a curtain wall or a curtain system is built from - its panels, its mullions by type, and how many grid lines run each way. It changes nothing. **A CURTAIN SYSTEM IS READ FACE BY FACE (version 3).** A curtain system made By Face on a mass holds one curtain grid for each face, and each face is read the way a curtain wall is - how many panels a curtain system has, its mullions and its panel sizes - under its own heading, "face 1 of 3". It answers the panels of a curtain system that already exists; making one is CREATE_CURTAIN_SYSTEM's. **IT EXISTS BECAUSE THE QUESTION WAS BEING ANSWERED BY `CREATE_WALL`.** Measured before this batch, *"what panels and mullions are in this curtain wall"* resolved to the fragment that BUILDS A WALL - a question about an existing element answered by making a new one. **A CURTAIN WALL IS THE ONE WALL WITH NO LAYERS, AND THIS IS ITS OTHER HALF.** `REPORT_COMPOUND_STRUCTURE` correctly reports that a curtain wall has no build-up. That is a true answer and an unhelpful one on its own: the wall IS made of something, and it is panels and mullions. The two fragments carry each other's row for that reason. **A PANEL IS NOT ALWAYS A `Panel`.** A curtain grid cell can hold a basic wall instead of a curtain panel family - that is how a solid infill or a spandrel is normally modelled - and it comes back in `GetPanelIds` like any other cell. Counting only `Panel` elements under-reports the wall and makes a glazing takeoff look short. Both kinds are counted, and the wall-as-panel ones are named separately because they are the ones a glass order must not include. **AN EMPTY CELL IS A REAL STATE.** A grid cell whose panel has been deleted returns an id that resolves to nothing. It is a hole in the elevation, and it is reported as one rather than skipped - a skipped null and a solid wall look identical in a count. **MULLIONS ARE GROUPED BY TYPE, WHICH IS WHAT GETS ORDERED.** Forty mullions is not a purchase order; twelve of one profile and twenty-eight of another is. **PANEL SIZES (version 2).** Each panel's Width and Height, read off Revit, grouped within a tolerance - per wall, and across every wall handed in. A panel whose size Revit does not give is named, never guessed.

<a id="report-curtain-wall-type"></a>

### Report curtain wall type

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-11-24 (Revit 2024).

**What it does:** a curtain wall type's settings read back - grid layout and spacing, mullion types, Automatically Embed on or off, Join Condition.

Reads what a curtain wall TYPE is set to - for its Vertical Grid and its Horizontal Grid, the Layout, the Spacing in millimetres and Adjust for Mullion Size, and for its Vertical and Horizontal Mullions, the Interior, Border 1 and Border 2 types by "Family: Type" name, or none - its Construction settings, whether Automatically Embed is ticked and the Join Condition, and how many placed walls use the type. It changes nothing. **AUTOMATICALLY EMBED IS A QUESTION, SO IT IS ANSWERED HERE.** "Is automatically embed on for this curtain wall type" is read, never handed to SET_CURTAIN_WALL_EMBED, which ticks the box (D-86). The box is read by its id, ALLOW_AUTO_EMBED, and answered yes, no or NOT READ - a box that could not be read is never reported as unticked (D-52). The Join Condition is printed as Revit displays it, beside the number it holds and the id that answered: Revit labels two ids "Join Condition", AUTO_JOIN_CONDITION_WALL and AUTO_JOIN_CONDITION, and which one a curtain wall type carries is asked of the type, _WALL first, rather than assumed. **IT EXISTS BECAUSE THE QUESTIONS WERE LANDING ON WRITES.** Measured through the host's own find on 2026-09-24: once SET_CURTAIN_WALL_GRID and SET_CURTAIN_WALL_MULLIONS existed, "what is the grid spacing on this curtain wall" and "which mullion type is on the curtain wall borders" reached them - a question handed to something that changes the model (D-86). Nothing read these settings, so the writers' own cards were the nearest text. **EVERY SETTING IS READ BY REVIT'S OWN PARAMETER ID, NEVER BY A NAME.** On a curtain wall type each of these names appears twice, once per direction, and a lookup by name returns one of the two with no rule for which (D-54 s3, FRAGMENT-ISSUES 5b-203). READ_ELEMENT_PARAMETERS reads by name, so it cannot answer these reliably; this reads SPACING_LAYOUT_VERT and _HORIZ, SPACING_LENGTH_VERT and _HORIZ, CURTAINGRID_ADJUST_BORDER_VERT and _HORIZ, and the six AUTO_MULLION ids. **THE LAYOUT IS REPORTED TWICE, AND THE TWO ARE COMPARED.** Revit stores it as a whole number. It is named here by what SpacingRuleLayout calls that number - None 0, Fixed Distance 1, Fixed Number 2, Maximum Spacing 3, Minimum Spacing 5 - and printed beside the words Revit displays for it. A number displayed as a DIFFERENT layout is listed in `layoutsDisagreeing`: SET_CURTAIN_WALL_GRID writes those numbers on the assumption that this parameter uses them, and this is the read that can show the assumption wrong without writing anything. A Spacing under a layout that does not use one is said to do nothing. Under Fixed Number the count is each placed wall's own Number, which a type does not hold, and the answer says so. **THE TYPE IS NAMED, AS FOR THE TWO WRITERS** - "Curtain Wall: Storefront", or the bare type name when no other wall type shares it (D-54). REPORT_CURTAIN_ELEMENTS prints a placed wall's name, which is its type's. A basic or stacked wall type is refused by name. A curtain SYSTEM is out of scope: its type is a curtain system type, not a wall type, and the add-in refuses its name before this runs - nothing reads a curtain system's settings yet. **THE REACH IS COUNTED**, as the two writers count it: how many placed walls use the type, which is how many a change to any of these settings would change.

**How to use it**

1. Open the model in Revit and connect Heron: press **Heron** on the Heron tab, so its heron turns orange.
2. In a Claude chat, ask in your own words, for example *"what is the grid spacing on this curtain wall"*. Say the values under **You say** in the same sentence.
3. Heron answers in the chat. Nothing in the model changes.

Other ways to ask: *"is automatically embed on for this curtain wall"* · *"which mullion type is on the curtain wall borders"*
